PMGT1711 Week 06

PMGT1711 Week 06 - Directional Complexity, the Viable System Model and PESTLE

Overview

Some projects fail not because the technology is unknown or the network of tasks is huge, but because nobody agrees on where the project is going. This week covers:

• Directional complexity: projects with no consistently understood or agreed direction, unclear or undefined goals, or progress hampered by undisclosed political motivations and hidden agendas.

• Where the ambiguity sits in structural, technical and directional complexity, and why directional complexity shows a large problem space but a small solution space.

• Four complexity-theory perspectives on directionally complex projects: order and chaos, communication and structure, sensitivity to initial conditions, and control.

• Management approaches and named tools: dialogue, appreciative inquiry, critical systems heuristics and value management.

• How sponsors, project managers, teams, budgets, schedules, risk management and procurement behave when goals are still unsettled.

• The Viable System Model (VSM) of Stafford Beer: five functions any viable system must perform, recursion, and its diagnostic use.

• PESTLE, a checklist of external drivers (political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental), illustrated with the Sydney Metro West project.

Key Concepts

What directional complexity is

Directional complexity is found in projects where there is no consistently understood or agreed direction for the project, where goals are unclear or undefined, or where progress towards superficially agreed goals is being hampered by undisclosed political motivations and hidden agendas.

The core questions in such a project are "How do we share understanding?" and "How do we agree about what we have to do?" The distinguishing uncertainty is about what and why, not about how.

Diagnostic signals

Typical signs that a project is directionally complex:

• People say "we are not on the same page", "no one is listening", "why are we doing this?", "talking but not communicating".

• People nod in agreement but mean different things by the same words; hidden agendas and political motivations drive decisions; meetings produce argument instead of work starting.

• Common in organisational-change projects: something must improve, but what must improve is not clear.

• The standard project-management assumption - clarify goals early, align stakeholder information, then execute the agreed plan - does not hold.

• Achieving a workable direction can itself be half the success. The direction depends on cultural and interpersonal alignment, not on technical design.

• The prevailing feeling is "if only we knew what to do, we could deliver".

• Directional complexity may be known from the start, surface only later in planning, or appear mid-project when a new phenomenon emerges or an influential stakeholder changes their mind. Early on, the system may lack stable processes, hierarchy, direction or power relations.

Ambiguity should be resolved promptly, but never by forcing superficial consensus.

Where the ambiguity sits

Complexity has three factors: number of elements, interconnections and ambiguity. Structural projects have many elements whose relationships are fairly definite; directional and technical complexity can be severe even with few elements, because each element carries much more ambiguity.

Complexity type

Where the ambiguity lies

Structural

Time, cost, resources and the mass of dependencies

Technical

The technology and the solution (how to build it)

Directional

The problem definition, stakeholder needs and expectations, and the negotiated direction

In directional complexity the problem space is far larger than the solution space: goals, purposes and success criteria are undefined or contested, so it is not clear what would count as a solution at all. (Technical complexity is the mirror image: the goal is clear and the solution space is the unknown.) Strong interdependence means that a direction decision in one area changes the others, so ambiguity has to be handled as an interconnected whole. Cause-and-effect relations are hard to establish in such settings.

Four complexity-theory perspectives

Perspective

Key points

Order-chaos

The project sits closer to chaos than order: different stakeholders explore different peaks of the fitness landscape (the landscape of possible directions, where height represents how promising a direction looks). Until a sustainable consensus allows detailed planning, uncertainty has to be managed: "The system needs to find an order, not have one imposed on it." Authoritarian directives manufacture surface agreement while feedback amplifies hidden disagreement. But the project must not fall into total chaos either: partnering or alliances and executive sponsorship hold it together until a stable direction (and standard contracts) emerge

Communication and structure

Conflicting views and strong personalities produce heated, ineffective argument. What must be structured is the process of exploration and discussion, not its predetermined content or outcomes. Problem-structuring methodologies help clarify goals and negotiate shared meaning

Sensitivity to initial conditions

Structure imposed early shapes how goals and meanings are formed, then becomes fixed and culturalised, ever harder to change. Keep communication structures in place while questions remain open, and settle only what has matured. The project manager must acknowledge what is not yet known rather than pretend to certainty

Control

A sustainable structure may not exist yet, so the core of control is continuous communication: "If communication breaks down during periods of directional complexity, so will the project."

Complex adaptive system concepts applied to direction

Complex adaptive system concept

What it looks like in directional complexity

Hierarchy

Goals passed down the hierarchy become vague or inconsistent

Communication

Meaning itself is contested

Control

Vision-setting rather than metric-chasing

Emergence

A negotiated direction - or drift

Phase transition

Redefining the purpose changes the trajectory

Non-linearity

Small goal ambiguity amplifies into scattered effort

Adaptiveness

Goals are renegotiated and reframed

Initial conditions

The first framing of the vision shapes the direction

Recurring failure modes

• Activity for its own sake: building things to show progress produces rework, inappropriate solutions and dissatisfied stakeholders. If visible progress is needed, deliver only small sub-projects that are certainly required.

• Premature implementation: do not build before an acceptable position and shared direction exist.

• Structure for comfort: do not impose structure merely to feel in control.

• False agreement: a nod or a signature is not shared meaning; returning to sense-making later is very hard.

• Dominated discussion: forceful voices suppress quiet dissent, reduce adoption, hide risks that excluded stakeholders would have spotted, weaken commitment and cause later conflict, delay or abandonment. Inclusive discussion must be protected.

Frameworks and Formulas

Methods and tools for managing direction

Give goal exploration its own time and space. Use flexible, interpretive approaches built on soft rather than hard or closed systems thinking: knowledge emerges through dialogue, shared meaning, documents and exploratory modelling, while rigid processes can backfire. Named tools include:

• Dialogue: builds the trust and openness that shared understanding needs.

• Appreciative Inquiry: drives discovery and shared understanding by focusing on achievements, strengths, innovation, potential and valuable futures, connecting the different stakeholder groups.

• Critical systems heuristics: a framework for surfacing inconsistent or competing political agendas - who benefits, who decides, and whose claims are legitimate.

• Value Management / value engineering: functional analysis combined with creative, analytic and evaluative methods to optimise value and refine requirements. It is usually applied after agreement exists, but it can also pull conflicting stakeholders into joint problem-solving, removing unnecessary cost without sacrificing safety, quality, environmental compliance or functional requirements.

Fully identifying stakeholders and tracking their needs is the foundation of all of this.

Critical phases, sponsor, project manager and team

• Critical phases: early definition and agreement; avoid premature detailed planning. A study of 448 projects (Dvir and Lechler, 2004) found that the negative impact of changes in direction and goals can exceed the benefits of good planning - so explore the goals thoroughly before committing.

• Sponsor: obtains strategic information, communicates the political agenda, and protects the team from premature milestones and inappropriate deliverables. The analogy is an artistic director supporting experimental ballet: choreographer, composer, designer and dancers explore together until the vision takes shape, and only then does production and rehearsal begin. Trust, guidance and interim support matter throughout.

• Project manager: must be comfortable with ambiguity and with the absence of apparent control; explains that uncertainty is normal; communicates the ambiguity in an accessible way without hiding it; looks at the whole from several perspectives; and recognises when goals have become aligned enough to plan.

• Team: at the start there may be only one or two coordinators, with experts and advisers brought in as needed (media, sense-making, soft and critical systems, value studies, facilitation) rather than a full, resident, co-located delivery team.

Finance, schedule, risk and procurement under directional complexity

• Finance: realistic budgets require agreed goals and sufficient detail; early estimates may be little more than available funds plus guesswork, and their limitations must be explained to stakeholders. Control gates are review points, and their timing must flex beyond financial and reporting cycles: advance when goal agreement allows planning, not merely because a meeting has been held. "It is impossible to plan the unknown." A worked example traces budget estimates converging from a deviation of over 200% to 120% and then to 70% as goals were clarified - an illustration of convergence, not a prescribed contingency reserve.

• Schedule: for unclear goals, prefer milestone planning (Turner, 1999). Milestones act like periodic attractors - regular attention-focusing events that create urgency - but they need flexibility and cannot eliminate deliberate obstruction. The definition phase may be far longer than the delivery phase; once agreement is reached, implementation can be straightforward with little structural complexity.

• Risk: delivering an assumed goal before key stakeholders have agreed wastes resources and disengages people. Treat reaching agreement on the goal as the first project in a series of projects, and begin by revealing that different versions of the goal exist.

• Procurement: traditional contracts have to wait for clarified goals and a detailed plan. Until then prefer alliances and partnerships, and keep revisiting the critical success factors.

The Viable System Model (VSM)

Stafford Beer (author of Cybernetics and Management, 1959; Decision and Control, 1966; Brain of the Firm, 1972; Heart of the Enterprise, 1979) developed the Viable System Model in the tradition of cybernetics - the study of how systems steer and regulate themselves.

• Viable means able to survive and adapt. The model names five jobs, not five people: any viable organisation must somehow perform all five functions.

• The model is diagnostic: map the existing organisation or project onto it and check that every necessary function is actually being performed. How roles map to functions depends on the situation; the model is not an official organisation chart.

• Recursion: "Every viable system contains and is contained in a viable system" - a work team is a viable system inside a project, which is inside an organisation. Recursion is a property of nesting, not an additional function.

System

Function

Key points

System 1 - operations

Day-to-day work and its local management

The autonomous operating units, each with its own local environment (for example a Glad Products wrap-and-bag division, or Johnson & Johnson baby care, over-the-counter medicines and medical devices). Effectiveness is measured quantitatively (for example sales), alongside capability, productivity and latency; productivity = actuality / capability. Like a reflex arc: the spinal cord is the System 1 unit, sensory nerves carry market data, motor nerves carry actions that affect the market

System 2 - coordination

Prevents oscillation and conflict between System 1 units

When a plastic shortage made units compete, trust broke down, informal local rules appeared and communication failed; the coordinator takes the problem across divisions for assessment. Coordination is not the final policy authority

System 3 - internal control

The highest autonomous level and lowest corporate management; stabilises the internal environment

Issues directives downward, receives operational information upward; reallocates resources, restructures, breaks down departmental barriers. Systems 1-2 give local homeostasis (self-regulating stability); System 3 gives organic homeostasis, informed by System 4. Homeostasis means keeping stable while still changing - not freezing everything

System 4 - intelligence (development)

Gathers external information and integrates and converts the information rising from operations for System 5 decisions

Looks outward and forward, with a view of the wider environment (see PESTLE below). System 5's policy flows down to Systems 1-3, and System 5 needs System 4's accurate picture of reality

System 5 - identity and policy

Purpose, ethos, ultimate authority, values, identity, principles

Mediates between System 3 (current delivery) and System 4 (future adaptation), keeping the whole viable

A simplified schematic of the layering (functions and feedback channels, not a complete wiring diagram):

          [S5 Policy]
              |
       [S4 Development / Intelligence] --- wider environment (PESTLE)
              |
   [S3 Operational Control (+ Service Management)] --- 3* Audit ---+
              |                                                     |
      <S2 Coordination>                                             |
              |                                                     v
       [S1 unit] --- local environment      [S1 unit] --- local environment

The line marked 3* Audit is the audit channel by which System 3 checks what the operating units are really doing.

Why the model helps. It makes the roles of policy, coordination and adaptation explicit; it exposes gaps (for example, plenty of System 1 delivery but very little System 4 scanning); it forces a balance between System 3's short term and System 4's future; and it locates whether a disagreement is about policy (System 5), internal control (System 3) or scanning (System 4). Crucially, System 4 discovers and interprets change while System 5 holds the authority to set direction - scanning alone cannot determine the goal.

PESTLE: external drivers

Letter

Category

P - Political

Government, policy and regulatory agendas

E - Economic

Funding, budgets, markets

S - Social

Community, culture, public expectations

T - Technological

New technologies, competing technologies, IT

L - Legal

Law, contracts, compliance

E - Environmental

Nature, heritage, sustainability, climate

PESTLE is used to identify the external threats and opportunities behind stakeholder positions. For each factor ask: could this change the direction, or change what "success" looks like? It feeds System 4 of the Viable System Model: it makes external influences explicit and depersonalises disagreement (turning "you versus me" into a shared external environment). It identifies pressure; it does not automatically produce consensus.

Ashby's Law of Requisite Variety

A principle from cybernetics that underpins regulation in any viable system:

• Variety means the number of distinguishable elements or states. Write D for the disturbances hitting a system, R for its regulatory responses, and Z for the residual outcomes left after regulation.

• A simplified counting form of the law states Var(Z) >= Var(D) / Var(R), together with the maxim "Only variety can absorb variety". Here Var counts distinguishable states; it is not statistical variance, and this is a simplified cardinality expression rather than a universal statistical equation.

• In practice: the regulator needs enough varied and appropriately matched responses for the relevant disturbances. Attenuation reduces the variety of disturbances that reach the system; amplification increases the variety of responses available. A long list of possible responses without effective execution is not enough.

Worked Examples

Sydney Metro West: contested purpose

Sydney Metro West is a 24-kilometre underground railway line connecting Parramatta with the Sydney central business district. It shows every symptom of directional complexity: political quick wins and election timetables, a Treasury pushing cost control, communities demanding particular station locations, and some stakeholders framing the project as property development rather than transport. The purpose was therefore contested, and scope and value for money remained disputed.

The public figures illustrate why a disputed baseline complicates assessment. The project was announced in 2016 and construction began in 2020. A 2030 opening target was pushed back to 2032 after a 2023 review. Cost commitments and estimates over time: 6.4 billion Australian dollars committed in 2019; about 20 billion estimated by late 2019; 25.3 billion after the 2023 review - described as an overrun of at least 12 billion against a confidential business-case baseline. These commitments and estimates are not automatically comparable baselines. The right lesson is not that directionally complex projects can never avoid delay or overrun; it is that without an agreed baseline, judging delay and cost becomes itself a contested exercise.

Mapping roles onto the Viable System Model

In a project organisation, the five functions can map roughly as follows (one function can span several roles, and one role can serve several functions):

• System 1: site supervisors and workstream team members - the people doing the work.

• System 2: the project coordinator - smoothing clashes between workstreams.

• System 3: the project manager, with resource and budget control.

• System 4: the risk manager, steering committee and environmental scanning - looking outward and forward.

• System 5: the executive sponsor and the project vision - identity and policy.

A body analogy: organs (System 1), coordinated reflexes (System 2), regulation of the present state (System 3), eyes and ears (System 4), self and identity (System 5). The mapping is an argument to be justified by actual responsibilities, not an official classification - especially for procurement and steering roles. A good test of the mapping: if the direction changed suddenly, or government halved the budget, or a new minister changed the purpose, or a community campaign forced a redesign - who would notice first (System 4), who would have the authority to reset direction (System 5), and who would reallocate resources (System 3)?

The ballet analogy for sponsorship

An artistic director supports experimental ballet: choreographer, composer, designer and dancers explore together until the vision takes shape, and only then do production and rehearsal begin. The sponsor of a directionally complex project plays the same role - protecting the exploratory phase, providing trust, guidance and interim support, and not demanding premature deliverables. The lesson: agree on where the project is going before fixing how to build it; let direction emerge, then lock in structure; when goals are disputed, communication is the core control mechanism.
